name: Radioactive lipstick (Dr. Alfred Curie)

card.summary: 1930s French radium cosmetics sold under the name of a Dr Alfred Curie, marketed with the promise that radioactivity would energise skin and give a youthful, glowing look.
card.note: Historical product; radium cosmetics were restricted in France in 1937 and are not sold today.

quick.overview:
Tho-Radia was a French cosmetics brand launched in Paris in 1932 whose creams and other products contained radium and thorium. Packaging cited the formula of a Dr Alfred Curie, a physician who shared a surname with Pierre and Marie Curie but was not related to them.

Advertising showed a glowing young woman and promised that small doses of radioactivity would revitalise skin. Radium cosmetics belonged to a wider early-twentieth-century enthusiasm for radioactive products, and are now a historical example of a beauty fad.
quick.how: The brand sold creams and other toiletries to be applied to the skin. A July 1932 analysis found about 0.223 micrograms of radium bromide per 100 grams of cream. The products are no longer sold.
quick.risks: Radium and thorium are radioactive. French rules in 1937 limited radioactive materials to medical prescription with warning labels, and the company re-registered the brand without mentioning radium or Curie.

lead: Tho-Radia was a French cosmetics company active from 1932 to 1968 whose early products contained radium and thorium. It was created by pharmacist Alexis Moussalli, who partnered with a physician named Alfred Curie, and packaging read 'after Dr Alfred Curie's formula'. [1]

Alfred Curie had the same surname as Pierre and Marie Curie but was not related to them, and the Curies reportedly considered legal action. [1] Wikipedia's page on radioactive quackery lists Tho-Radia as a radium bromide powder or cream sold under the doctor's name. [2]
The products were sold for their supposed ability to energise skin and give a youthful look, drawing on the era's fascination with radium. [1][3]

chain: Cream or cosmetic containing radium and thorium
Marketing: small radioactive doses energise skin cells
angle.text: The brand promised anti-ageing and revitalising effects from radioactivity. This is documented as a historical product; the idea that tiny radium doses energise living cells was never scientifically demonstrated.

paras: Tho-Radia launched in Paris in 1932 and reached the rest of France in 1933. Its adverts featured a young blond woman lit from below by visible rays, a look that lasted into the 1950s. [1]

New French rules in 1937 restricted radioactive materials to medical prescription and required warning labels. The company re-registered the brand without mentioning radium or Alfred Curie. Moussalli died in 1955, the firm was sold to Lafarge laboratories in 1962, and the brand was abandoned in 1968. [1]

Radium appeared in several cosmetic brands of the era, including Artes, Ramey, Radior and Tho-Radia, marketed with anti-aging promises. [3] Radioactive quackery more broadly peaked in the early twentieth century after the 1896 discovery of radioactivity, and included Radithor, whose heavy use by industrialist Eben Byers was followed by his death in 1932. [2]
